ownerThemes.theme: One owner who replaced a Baby Lock coverstitch says it has never skipped a stitch; others say it is finicky and skips until needles are fresh and matched to the fabric.
Long discussion thread ranges from 'greatest machine ever' to 'want to throw it out the window'; the split tracks with setup, needle choice and stabilizer on thin knits.

crossShop.why: The other mainstream dedicated coverstitch; wider bed, free arm and a tension release lever for a few hundred more.
A serger and coverstitch combo at a similar price for buyers who cannot fit two machines.
Owners typically pair the 2340CV with a 1034D as a two-machine setup.

editorial.verdict: The 2340CV is the lowest-priced dedicated coverstitch from a major brand: 3-needle, 3 or 6 mm cover stitch plus chain stitch at 1,100 spm.
editorial.whoFor: A knit sewist who owns a serger and wants ready-to-wear style hems without buying a combo machine.
editorial.skipIf: You need a free arm, a tension release lever, or a wider bed; the Janome CoverPro 2000CPX has those.
editorial.keySpec: 1/2/3 needle · 3 or 6 mm cover · chain stitch · 1,100 spm
strengths: Standard 130/705H household needles, so ball points for knits are easy to source.

weaknesses: No automatic tension release, a frequent owner complaint when removing work.

checks.title: Needles for knits
checks.body: The manual names SCHMETZ 130/705H 90/14 and recommends SUK ball point for knits. Buy ball points before the first project.

checks.title: Two feet in the box
checks.body: Standard foot and a hem foot. Binders, clear feet and belt loop folders are add-ons, often bundled by dealers.

checks.title: It is not a serger
checks.body: Retail titles say 'coverstitch serger'. It has no knife and no overlock stitch. You still need a serger or a sewing machine for seams.

realCost: 3 to 4 cones of thread; a wooly nylon for the looper is optional
